claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are initially solid.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are well-mixed, disordered solid solutions.
Rapid thermal-shock synthesis can produce the stated well-mixed FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Local composition gradients occur at the nanoparticle surfaces.
Local surface compositional variations create heterogeneous surface energies.
Local deviations in surface elemental distribution lower the local melting temperature.
Premelting initiates selectively at compositionally inhomogeneous surface regions.
Early surface premelting propagates inward and triggers melting of the nanoparticle core.
Compositionally inhomogeneous nanoparticles will begin melting earlier than more compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
Compositionally inhomogeneous nanoparticles will exhibit spatially non-uniform surface melting.
Initially homogeneous nanoparticles will melt uniformly near the predicted bulk melting point.
In situ electron microscopy and synchrotron X-ray diffraction are applicable to heated multielement nanoparticles.
Heating rate may influence the proposed premelting effect.
An inert or vacuum environment prevents surface oxidation during the test.
High-temperature exposure in microscope vacuum can cause elemental evaporation from multielement nanoparticles.
The magnitude of the melting-temperature shift may vary with nanoparticle size, heating rate, and the magnitude of compositional deviations.
Controlled partial annealing or chemical treatment can intentionally enhance local compositional segregation in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
A lack of correlation between initial composition gradients and premelting onset would falsify the proposed governing role of those gradients.

contradictions.description: The starting particles are described as well-mixed and homogeneous, while the proposed mediator requires local surface compositional variations in the particles whose transition is being explained. The hypothesis does not state whether such gradients already coexist with bulk homogeneity, arise during heating, or apply only to the intentionally segregated comparison set.
